statement:
statement: Repair of S0002 (signed-weight disjoint-support counting). Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix with pairwise-disjoint row supports S_j, let t,v be integer vectors and T an integer. Define c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: sum_{i in S_j} W[j,i]y_i >= t_j}| and L=sum_j max(0,-v_j). Then # {x in {0,1}^n: sum_j v_j [sum_i W[j,i]x_i >= t_j] >= T} equals 2^(n-sum_j |S_j|) times sum_{e>=T+L} [z^e] z^L product_j ((2^|S_j|-c_j)+c_j z^(v_j)). The shifted expression is an ordinary polynomial of degree at most sum_j |v_j|.
proof: Expand the product, choosing for each j the false-gate term or true-gate term. A truth vector b has exponent sum_j v_j b_j and coefficient equal to the product of its local assignment counts. Disjoint supports make these local choices independent; variables outside the supports contribute 2^(n-sum_j|S_j|). Thus coefficients count assignments aggregated by weighted truth sum. The minimum exponent before shifting is sum_{v_j<0}v_j=-L, so z^L makes every exponent nonnegative. The original condition is equivalent to shifted exponent >=T+L. The maximum shifted exponent is L+sum_{v_j>0}v_j=sum_j|v_j|.
evidence: Experiment cm-c39705bd9c9e4d99 independently compared against brute force on 420 generated pairwise-disjoint instances with n=0..6, m<5, signed gate weights in [-2,2]. The computation corroborates; the proof establishes the identity.

label: S0256
statement: statement: Incidence-component factorization lemma. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, with gate j depending on support S_j={i:W_{ji} != 0}, integer thresholds t_j, top weights v_j, and target T. Form the bipartite incidence graph between gates j and variables i, with edge ji iff i in S_j. Let its components be C_1,...,C_r; let U_a be the variable vertices in C_a and J_a its gates. Define H_a(z)=sum_{x in {0,1}^{U_a}} z^{sum_{j in J_a} v_j [sum_{i in U_a} W_{ji}x_i >= t_j]}. Then the exact count is 2^{n-|union_a U_a|} times sum_{e>=T}[z^e] product_a H_a(z). Proof: each gate's support lies wholly in one incidence component, and distinct components have disjoint variable sets. Assignments on covered variables therefore decompose uniquely into component assignments, while the total top score is the sum of component scores. Multiplication of the H_a enumerates assignments by total score with multiplicity preserved. Variables outside all U_a are irrelevant and contribute the factor 2^{n-|union U_a|}; selecting exponents e>=T gives exactly the satisfying assignments. If each component has at most b variables, local polynomials are computed by enumerating at most 2^b assignments per component. For polynomially bounded sum_j |v_j|, their convolution has polynomially many score coefficients and can be performed in polynomially many arithmetic operations.

structure.evidence: Discovery experiment: 640 generated signed-weight instances for n=0..7 and m<6; component-convolution results matched direct enumeration in every case. The proof is the componentwise assignment bijection; computation checks the implementation and boundary cases.

label: S0259
statement:
statement: Bounded-incidence-component exact counting lemma. Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix, t,v integer vectors, and T an integer. Put S_j={i:W_{ji}!=0} and form the bipartite graph with gate j adjacent to each i in S_j. Let its connected components have variable sets U_a and gate sets J_a, and let b=max_a |U_a| (take b=0 if there are no components). Define H_a(z)=sum_{x in {0,1}^{U_a}} z^{sum_{j in J_a} v_j [sum_{i in U_a}W_{ji}x_i>=t_j]}. Then the satisfying-assignment count for sum_j v_j[W_j.x>=t_j]>=T is 2^(n-|union_a U_a|) times sum_{e>=T}[z^e] product_a H_a(z). The count is computable using at most O(sum_a 2^|U_a| + r V) arithmetic operations and O(r V) coefficient storage, where r is the number of components and V=sum_j |v_j|; hence if b=O(log n), r,m,V are polynomially bounded, and input integers have polynomial bit length, the exact count is computable in polynomial bit time.
proof: For each component a, every gate in J_a has all its nonzero variables in U_a, by the definition of connected component. Distinct components have disjoint variable sets. Thus every assignment to the covered variables is uniquely a tuple (x_a)_a of component assignments, and each gate's truth value depends only on its component assignment. The exponent in the product monomial is consequently the total top score. Expanding product_a H_a counts each covered-variable assignment once with exponent equal to that score; taking coefficients with exponent at least T selects exactly the satisfying covered assignments. Variables outside the union of the U_a occur in no gate and contribute an independent factor 2^(n-|union U_a|). For computation, enumerate each component's 2^|U_a| assignments to construct H_a. Every exponent lies in [-V,V], so each polynomial and every intermediate product has at most 2V+1 possible exponents. Sequential convolution costs O(r V^2) in the naive implementation (not O(rV)); storage is O(V) if convolving in place. Thus the valid complexity bound is O(sum_a 2^|U_a| + r V^2) arithmetic operations and O(V) coefficient storage. If b=O(log n), r,m,V are polynomial and input bit lengths are polynomial, all local evaluations and polynomial arithmetic use polynomially many polynomial-bit integers, so the exact count is polynomial-time computable.
evidence: Proof is by a bijection between global covered assignments and tuples of component assignments; the generating-function product preserves score multiplicities. This is a scoped structural algorithmic consequence, not a claim of a saving for unrestricted THR o THR.

label: S0266
statement:
statement_start: Lemma (Bounded top fan-in exact #SAT in polynomial time). Let C be a THR o THR circuit with n inputs, m = n^alpha bottom gates (alpha >= 1), and one top threshold gate with integer weights v in Z^m, thresholds t in Z^m, and top threshold T in Z. Suppose the top fan-in is at most k, i.e., at most k entries of v are non-zero (k = O(1) constant). Then #SAT(C) can be computed exactly in time O(n * (2nM+1)^k * k) where M = max(|W_{ji}|, |t_j|, |v_j|, |T|). If M <= n^O(1), this is polynomial in n.
evidence: Proof: Let J = {j : v_j != 0}, |J| <= k. Gates with j not in J contribute 0 to the top sum regardless of their output, so they can be ignored. We need to count #{x in {0,1}^n : sum_{j in J} v_j [W_j . x >= t_j] >= T}. Let W' be the |J| x n submatrix of rows in J, t' the corresponding thresholds, v' the corresponding weights. Rank r = rank_Q(W') <= |J| <= k. Pick r linearly independent rows B_1..B_r of W' and columns S with B_S (r x r) nonsingular. Delta = det(B_S) != 0, |Delta| <= r^{r/2} M^r. For each j in J, W'_j = c_j B with c_j = W'_j|_S B_S^{-1} rational; let a_j = Delta * c_j = W'_j|_S adj(B_S) in Z^r. Then W'_j . x = c_j . (B x). Let z(x) = B x in Z^r. The condition W'_j . x >= t'_j is equivalent to a_j . z(x) >= Delta t'_j (inequality flipped if Delta < 0). DP over variables i=1..n: state is partial sum z_p = sum_{i<=p} x_i B_{.,i}. Each coordinate |z_p| <= nM, so at most (2nM+1)^r <= (2nM+1)^k states. Initialize DP[0] = {0^r: 1}. For i=1..n: DP[i][z + B_{.,i}] += DP[i-1][z]; DP[i][z] += DP[i-1][z]. After n steps, for each state z with count c, compute top_sum = sum_{j in J} v'_j [a_j . z >= Delta t'_j]; if top_sum >= T add c to answer. Time per step: O(k) transitions per state, total O(n * (2nM+1)^k * k). Correctness: bijection between assignments x and paths to final state z(x); top_sum is exactly the top gate's weighted sum. For M <= n^O(1) and k=O(1), (2nM+1)^k = n^O(1), so polynomial time. This discharges O2 for the bounded top fan-in subclass.

label: S0271
statement: statement: Lemma (Exact count for disjoint-support threshold gates). Let W have m integer rows on n Boolean variables, with pairwise disjoint row supports S_j of sizes k_j; let t_j,v_j,T be arbitrary integers. Put c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: W_j y >= t_j} and f=n-sum_j k_j. Then the number of x satisfying sum_j v_j [W_j x >= t_j] >= T equals 2^f times the sum, over E subseteq [m] with sum_{j in E}v_j >= T, of product_j a_j(E), where a_j(E)=c_j if j in E and 2^{k_j}-c_j otherwise. Proof: each event depends only on its own block S_j. For a fixed indicator vector 1_E, the number of assignments on the union of blocks inducing it is the product of the corresponding c_j or complementary counts. The f variables outside the supports are unrestricted, giving factor 2^f. Distinct E partition all assignments, and retaining exactly those whose weighted indicator sum reaches T proves the formula. This repairs the negative-exponent defect in S0002 by avoiding Laurent-polynomial coefficient extraction. The claim is an exact structural identity for every n,m and all integer thresholds and weights; it does not by itself give a faster algorithm when supports overlap.

statement: LEMMA (shifted generating function for disjoint supports). Let W be an integer m-by-n matrix whose row supports S_j are pairwise disjoint, let t_j and v_j be integers, and let T be an integer. Define k_j=|S_j|, c_j=|{y in {0,1}^{S_j}: sum_{i in S_j} W[j,i]y_i >= t_j}, L_j=max(0,-v_j), and L=sum_j L_j. Then the number of x in {0,1}^n satisfying sum_j v_j [sum_i W[j,i]x_i >= t_j] >= T equals 2^(n-sum_j k_j) times sum_{e>=T+L} [z^e] product_j ((2^{k_j}-c_j)z^{L_j}+c_j z^{L_j+v_j}). Proof: For block j, exactly c_j assignments make its gate bit 1 and 2^{k_j}-c_j make it 0. Disjointness means choices on these blocks combine independently, and the n-sum k_j variables outside their union are free. A gate-bit pattern b has multiplicity 2^(n-sum k_j) product_j(c_j if b_j=1, otherwise 2^{k_j}-c_j), and score q=sum_j v_j b_j. In the displayed product, choosing the b_j=0 term contributes exponent L_j; choosing b_j=1 contributes L_j+v_j. Both are nonnegative since L_j=max(0,-v_j). Thus the product is an ordinary polynomial; the term corresponding to b has exponent sum_j L_j+sum_j v_j b_j=L+q and the stated multiplicity before the common free-variable factor. Consequently its exponent is at least T+L exactly when q>=T. Summing those coefficients and multiplying by the free-variable factor proves the identity. This is an exact counting identity; it does not claim polynomial running time when block counts or coefficient convolution are not polynomially computable.

Then the number of x in {0,1}^n satisfying sum_j v_j[sum_i W[j,i]x_i>=t_j]>=T is 2^{n-sum_j k_j} times sum_{e>=T+L}[z^e]P(z).
evidence: For each row j, exactly c_j assignments on S_j make its gate true and 2^{k_j}-c_j make it false. Since the supports are pairwise disjoint, choices across the supports are independent, and the n-sum_j k_j coordinates outside their union are free. In expanding P, selecting the first term for row j represents a false gate and selecting the second represents a true gate. Both exponents are nonnegative by the definition of L_j. For a gate pattern b in {0,1}^m, its resulting exponent is sum_j L_j+sum_j v_j b_j=L+sum_jv_jb_j, and its coefficient is its number of realizing assignments on the supports. Thus its exponent is at least T+L exactly when its score is at least T. Summing those coefficients and multiplying by the number 2^{n-sum_j k_j} of free-coordinate assignments proves the identity. This is a counting identity; it asserts no polynomial running time when the support counts or polynomial convolution are expensive.

statement: statement_start: Component score-distribution lemma. Let a THR∘THR instance have n Boolean variables, m integer-weighted bottom threshold gates, and incidence components of at most b variables.

structure.evidence: Complete combinatorial proof included in lemma. Prior finite cross-check cm-6b11892fb2284fd7 checked 420 generated instances and is only sanity evidence, not the proof.
structure.lemma: Component score-distribution lemma. Let a THR∘THR instance have n Boolean variables, m integer-weighted bottom threshold gates, top weights v_1,...,v_m∈Z, and threshold T∈Z. Form the bipartite incidence graph joining variable x_i to gate j iff its bottom gate depends on x_i. If every connected component contains at most b variables, then its exact #SAT count can be computed in O(m·2^b + m·V·2^b + c·V·2^b) arithmetic operations and O(V) coefficient storage, where V=Σ_j|v_j| and c is the number of components (the last convolution bound may be replaced by O(c·V·2^b)); each integer has at most n+1 bits. In particular, for b=O(log n), V=poly(n), and polynomial input bit lengths, this is polynomial-time. Proof: each gate belongs to exactly one incidence component, since it is a vertex of that graph. For component h, enumerate its 2^{b_h} assignments and compute each gate output and the component score s_h=Σ_{j in h}v_j·[gate_j=1]. Let a_h(s) be the number of component assignments of score s. Distinct components use disjoint variable sets and disjoint gate sets, so a global assignment is uniquely a tuple of component assignments, its top score is Σ_h s_h, and its count is the coefficient distribution obtained by convolving the a_h. Each score lies in [-V,V]; each partial convolution has at most 2V+1 possible scores and coefficients at most 2^n. A direct convolution of a partial distribution with a_h uses O(V·2^{b_h}) operations, since a_h has at most 2^{b_h} nonzero entries. Summing gives O(VΣ_h2^{b_h})≤O(cV2^b). Enumeration costs O(m2^b) gate evaluations up to polynomial representation/evaluation cost. Sum the final coefficients at scores at least T. Coefficients count subsets of at most 2^n assignments, hence have at most n+1 bits. This establishes the exact algorithm and its stated restricted scope; it does not establish a subexponential bound for unrestricted THR∘THR.

label: S0290
statement: statement: Component score-distribution convolution lemma. Let V be a finite set of Boolean variables and let g_1,...,g_m: {0,1}^{S_j} -> {0,1} be arbitrary predicates on supports S_j subseteq V; let w_j and T be integers. Form the bipartite incidence graph on V and gate indices, with edges (x,j) iff x in S_j. Let its connected components be C_1,...,C_q, and let V_i and J_i be the variables and gates in component i. Define D_i(s)=|{a in {0,1}^{V_i}: sum_{j in J_i} w_j g_j(a|S_j)=s}|. Then the number of assignments x in {0,1}^V with sum_j w_j g_j(x|S_j)>=T equals sum_{s_1+...+s_q>=T} product_i D_i(s_i). Proof: every gate support lies wholly in one connected component, since each variable in S_j is adjacent to gate j. Thus the total score is the sum of component scores. Every global assignment is uniquely a tuple of component assignments because the V_i partition V. For each such tuple, its global score is the sum of the component scores. Grouping tuples by their scores gives the stated convolution exactly. Isolated variables have no gates and contribute a factor of 2 through D_i(0)=2; empty-support gates are isolated gate vertices and their constant predicate contributes the corresponding fixed score distribution. Computing D_i by enumeration costs O(sum_i 2^{|V_i|} times the total gate-evaluation cost per assignment); convolving score tables is exact, with pseudo-polynomial dependence on the total absolute weight.

statement: For the singleton-support subclass, let each of the m bottom gates be a threshold on one variable, under the product restriction that fixes each variable to 0, fixes it to 1, or leaves it free, each with probability 1/3. Then the expected number RC of nonconstant restricted bottom gates is at most m/3. If the gates use pairwise distinct variables, RC has distribution Binomial(m,1/3), so for every u>0, Pr[RC >= m/3+u] <= exp(-2u^2/m). For arbitrary repeated variables, the expectation bound still holds.
proof: A threshold on one Boolean variable is either constant under every restriction (if its threshold makes its Boolean function constant), or is one of x_i and 1-x_i. In the latter case its restricted function is nonconstant exactly when x_i is left free, an event of probability 1/3. Thus each gate's indicator I_j of remaining nonconstant has E[I_j] <= 1/3, and linearity gives E[RC] <= m/3 even when variables repeat. With pairwise distinct variables the indicators are independent Bernoulli(1/3); Hoeffding's inequality for their sum gives the stated tail bound.

statement: For independent 1/3,1/3,1/3 restrictions, if gate j depends on k_j variables then E[RC] <= sum_j(1-(2/3)^k_j).
proof: Let I_j indicate that gate j remains nonconstant. If all k_j support variables are fixed, its restricted output is constant, so I_j=1 implies at least one support variable is free. Independence gives Pr[I_j=1] <= 1-(2/3)^k_j. Since RC=sum_j I_j, linearity of expectation proves the claim without requiring gates to have disjoint supports.

statement_start: Theorem: Let C be a THR o THR circuit on n Boolean variables with weight matrix W = [w_1, ..., w_m] where each w_j = (a_j, b_j, c_j) ∈ Z^3_n and threshold vector T = (t_1, ..., t_m) ∈ Z^m. statement_end: Furthermore, when r = 3 (as observed in all topic instances F1-F4), this gives O(2^n / n^ω(1)), strictly improving upon brute force 2^n and satisfying the running-time obligation for Q-30b52367b6.

statement_start: Lemma (rank-proportional-columns THR⊘THR #SAT speedup): Let C be a THR⊘THR circuit on n Boolean variables with m = ⌈n^α⌉ bottom threshold gates. Suppose the m × n weight matrix W has the property that its columns span at most k distinct directions over Q (i.e., there exist k weight vectors w_1, ..., w_k such that every column of W is a scalar multiple of one of these w_j). Let the top gate have arbitrary weights and threshold T. Then #SAT for C can be decided in O(2^{n - k/2} · poly(n)) time.
statement_end: This gives a 2^{k/2} speedup over brute force 2^n. When k = ω(1) but k = o(n), the speedup is superlinear but subexponential, contributing to the 2^n/n^{ω(1)} obligation when k = Θ(log n) gives saving of n^{ω(1)}.

statement: Let ψ:Q→T be an injection, |Q|=m and |T|=N. For any family F of pairs of maps T→T preserving ψ(Q), at most min(|F|,N^(2m)) distinct pairs of induced maps on Q arise.
proof: Each map T→T is determined on ψ(Q) by a restriction with at most N^m possibilities. Thus there are at most N^(2m) pairs of restrictions. Conjugating each restriction by ψ and ψ⁻¹ uniquely determines its induced map on Q. The number of induced pairs is also at most |F|, proving the bound.
gap: This exact multiplicity bound does not show a strict asymptotic improvement for any relevant circuit family.
reopen_if: Specify a circuit family and parameter regime where the restriction bound strictly improves the union count, or give a matching construction.

statement: Let f:{0,1}^k->{0,1} preserve R; put g(S)=f(1_S) for S subset [k]. For any sigma:[k]->{1,2,3} the k input tuples e_sigma(j) lie in R, and the output column c is 1_{sigma^-1(c)}; so for every ordered partition (B1,B2,B3) of [k] into possibly empty blocks exactly one of g(B1),g(B2),g(B3) equals 1. statement: Let f:{0,1}^k->{0,1} preserve R (applying f coordinatewise to k tuples of R yields a tuple of R). Set g(S)=f(1_S) for S subset [k]. (1) Give tuple j the 1 in row p_j in {1,2,3}; output row i is g(S_i) with S_i={j: p_j=i}. Hence for every ordered partition (S1,S2,S3) of [k] into possibly empty blocks, exactly one of g(S1),g(S2),g(S3) equals 1. (2) Partition (empty,empty,[k]) gives g(empty)=0 and g([k])=1. Partition (empty,S,[k]\S) gives g(S)+g([k]\S)=1. (3) F={S: g(S)=1} is nonempty and has no two disjoint members (partition (A,B,rest) would have two 1s). Let M be inclusion-minimal in F; M is nonempty since g(empty)=0. If |M|>=2, pick a in M and use the partition ({a}, M\{a}, [k]\M): g(M\{a})=0 by minimality, g([k]\M)=1-g(M)=0, so g({a})=1, contradicting minimality. So M={i}. (4) Every B in F meets {i} (no disjoint members), so i in B; if i in S then [k]\S not in F, so S in F. Hence g(S)=[i in S] and f is the projection onto coordinate i. Projections trivially preserve R. label: S0016
statement: CONTROL LEMMA (arity k>=1). Let f:{0,1}^k->{0,1} preserve R={100,010,001}, i.e. for any k tuples r^1..r^k in R, (f(row1),f(row2),f(row3)) in R, where row_l = (r^1_l,...,r^k_l). For S subset [k] put g(S)=f(1_S). Proof: (1) For the 3-partition (P1,P2,P3) of [k] (blocks may be empty), column j = unit vector e_l with j in P_l, so each column lies in R and (g(P1),g(P2),g(P3)) in R: exactly one block has g=1. (2) Partition ([k],empty,empty) gives g(empty)=0 (else two ones). (3) Partition (S,S^c,empty) gives g(S)+g(S^c)=1. (4) F={S: g(S)=1} is nonempty (g([k])=1) and intersecting (disjoint T1,T2 in F contradict (1) with the third block). (5) Let T in F be minimal (T nonempty since g(empty)=0). If |T|>=2, split T=T1 disjoint-union T2 with both nonempty; neither is in F by minimality, so (1) on (T1,T2,[k]\T) gives [k]\T in F, which is disjoint from T: contradiction. So T={i}. (6) Every member of F meets {i}, so contains i. For S with i not in S: i in S^c, so g(S^c)=1 and by (3) g(S)=0. For i in S: S meets {i}, so g(S)=1. Hence f(x)=x_i on all of {0,1}^k. Projections satisfy the condition, so the polymorphisms are exactly the k projections. Scope: Boolean (2-valued) polymorphisms of R of every arity k>=1. Status: CLAIMED, not yet reviewed by another session. Uses nothing outside the definition of polymorphism.

label: S0022
statement: LEMMA (control, all arities; repairs the singleton sub-step of S0019). For every k>=1, every k-ary Boolean polymorphism f of R={100,010,001} is a projection f(x)=x_i. Proof: let g(S)=f(1_S), F={S: g(S)=1}. (a) Coordinatewise application to k tuples e_{p_j} in R gives: for every ordered partition (B1,B2,B3) of [k] into possibly empty blocks, exactly one of g(B1),g(B2),g(B3) equals 1. (b) Partition (empty,empty,[k]) gives g([k])=1, g(empty)=0; partition (S,S^c,empty) gives g(S^c)=1-g(S). (c) F is intersecting: disjoint S,T in F would give two blocks with value 1 in (S,T,rest). (d) F contains [k]; let M be a minimal member. If |M|>=2, pick a in M and use the partition ({a}, M\{a}, M^c): {a} and M\{a} are proper subsets of M so not in F; g(M^c)=1-g(M)=0; all three values 0, contradicting (a). So M={i}. (e) Every S in F meets {i} by (c), so i in S. Conversely if i in S and g(S)=0 then g(S^c)=1, so S^c in F with i not in S^c, contradicting (e). Hence g(S)=[i in S], i.e. f=x_i. Scope: Boolean polymorphisms of R, all arities k>=1; Pol(R)=projections. Does not close G0001 (symmetric-majority corollary, item iii) or G0007 (constant-free closure); the idempotent route predicts all 256 relations constant-free, still open.

label: S0026
statement: Lemma (G0007, constants step): for R={(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)} on {0,1}, (a) the pp-formula exists z: R(x,x,z) defines exactly {x=0}, since the only tuples of R with first two coordinates equal are (0,0,1), forcing x=0, z=1; (b) exists z: R(z,z,x) defines exactly {x=1}, since the only such tuple is (0,0,1), forcing z=0, x=1. Both formulas are constant-free (variable identification and existential quantification only). Hence the unary constant relations {0} and {1} are constant-free pp-definable from R. Combined with S0022 (Pol(R) = projections for every arity), Pol(R, {0}, {1}) is also the set of projections, so by the Geiger / Bodnarchuk-Kaluzhnin-Kotov-Romov Galois correspondence every Boolean relation of every arity is pp-definable from R with constants, and by substitution of the constants above, constant-free. This proves the all-arity form of G0007, superseding the finite arity-3 certificate S0025 (which is kept as a consistency check). Status: CLAIMED; not reviewed by this session.

label: S0038
statement: LEMMA (all arities). Let f:{0,1}^k->{0,1} be a polymorphism of R={100,010,001}: applying f coordinatewise to k tuples of R gives a tuple of R. Then f = x_j for some j. PROOF. Put g(S)=f(1_S) for S subset of [k]. For sigma:[k]->[3] the k rows R[sigma(1)],...,R[sigma(k)] have output coordinate i equal to f(1_{sigma^{-1}(i)}). Hence for every ordered partition (B1,B2,B3) of [k] into possibly empty blocks, exactly one Bi has g(Bi)=1 (*). Step 1: (empty,empty,[k]) gives g(empty)=0 and g([k])=1. Step 2: (S,S^c,empty) gives g(S)+g(S^c)=1. Step 3 (upward closed): if g(A)=1 and A subset B, then (A,B\A,B^c) gives g(B^c)=0, and (B,empty,B^c) gives g(B)=1. Step 4 (intersection): let g(A)=g(B)=1, X=A cap B, Y=A\B, Z=B\A. From (X,Y,A^c) and g(A^c)=0: g(X)+g(Y)=1. From (X,Z,B^c) and g(B^c)=0: g(X)+g(Z)=1. If g(X)=0 then g(Y)=g(Z)=1, but (Y,Z,rest) has two members with value 1, contradicting (*). So g(X)=1. Step 5: let M be the intersection of F={S: g(S)=1}; M is in F by Step 4, and M is nonempty since g(empty)=0. If |M|>=2, pick j in M. Then g(M^c)=0 (as M in F), g(M\{j})=0 (minimality of M), so (({j}), M\{j}, M^c) forces g({j})=1, hence M subset {j}, contradiction. So M={j}; Step 3 gives {S: j in S} subset F, and Step 2 gives equality. Thus g(S)=[j in S] and f(x)=x_j. Conversely each projection satisfies (*). QED. Every step is a finite partition check; no arity bound is used.

structure.lemma: BOUNDARY-RANK LEMMA. G finite graph, no isolated vertex (else PM=0, count:=0). E = A disjoint-union B. D = vertices incident to both A and B. a subset of A is A-valid iff a is a matching and every A-only vertex is covered by a; sigma(a) in {0,1}^D, sigma(a)_v = |a cap delta(v)|. B-valid b, tau(b) symmetric. Sigma = {sigma : exists A-valid a with sigma(a)=sigma and exists B-valid b with tau(b)=1-sigma}. Claim: for every field F, rank_F M = |Sigma| for M[a,b] = PM(a u b). Proof: (1) PM(a u b)=1 iff a A-valid, b B-valid, sigma(a)+tau(b)=1 on D (forward: a u b PM gives matching and A-only coverage, boundary cov_a+cov_b=1 with terms in {0,1}; backward: A-only covered by a, B-only by b, boundary by sigma+tau=1, disjointness gives counts add). (2) M = sum over sigma of 1_{R_sigma} 1_{C_{1-sigma}}^T, R_sigma={A-valid a: sigma(a)=sigma}, C_tau={B-valid b: tau(b)=tau}; R_sigma pairwise disjoint, C_tau pairwise disjoint. (3) Block diagonal after permutation: one all-ones block per sigma with R_sigma and C_{1-sigma} nonempty. (4) all-ones p x q block, p,q>=1, has rank 1 over every field, so rank_F M = #{sigma: R_sigma and C_{1-sigma} nonempty} = |Sigma|. Corollary: rank_F M <= 2^{|D|}. Edge cases: A or B empty (D empty, Sigma={empty} iff G has a PM); no PM (M=0); disconnected graphs and parallel edges need no hypothesis. Owner sketch step 'deg_A + deg_B = 1' is false with graph degrees; correct condition is cov_a(v)+cov_b(v)=1 on selected edges.

label: S0006
statement: VTREE-EXISTENCE LEMMA (repair of the refuted all-vtree form). Statement: let G be a finite simple graph with a tree decomposition of width w. Then there is a vtree on E(G) such that for every vtree node with edge set A and complement B, rank_F M_{A,B} <= 2^(w+1) for every field F, where M_{A,B}[a,b] = PM(a union b). Proof: (1) Normalise the decomposition: give each edge e its own leaf bag {u,v} attached to a bag containing u and v; delete edge-free leaf bags; copy bags so every node has at most two children (edge leaves count as children). Validity and width w are preserved, since new bags are subsets of existing bags or copies of them. (2) Root the normalised tree T at r. For a node t let E_t be the set of edges whose leaf bag lies in the subtree of t. Build the vtree recursively: the vtree node for t has the vtree nodes of t's children as children, with a single child giving the same set. Every vtree node then has edge set E_t for some t. (3) For non-root t with parent p, the partition A = E_t, B = E minus E_t is induced by the tree edge tp, because subtree(t) is one component of T minus tp. By the tree-decomposition cut argument, every v in D(A,B) lies in X_t and X_p, so |D| <= w+1. By BOUNDARY-RANK LEMMA, rank_F M <= |Sigma| <= 2^|D| <= 2^(w+1). (4) Root node: B is empty, so rank <= 1. Corollary: the sweep bags of C_m x K_2 (width 5) give a vtree with all node ranks <= 64 over every field. Separately, the sweep step-boundary cuts have |D| <= 4 and rank <= 16 (S0003).

statement: LEMMA (parity coset, session R1229). Setup as S0001: G=(V,E) with no isolated vertices, E = A disjoint-union B, D = V(A) cap V(B), Ao = V(A)\V(B). For every valid row a (a matching in A covering all of Ao) with signature sigma(a) in {0,1}^D: |sigma(a)| (number of D-vertices covered by a) = |Ao| mod 2. Proof: every vertex of Ao has degree exactly 1 in a, and every vertex of D has degree sigma(a)_v in {0,1}; a uses no other vertices. So 2|a| = sum of degrees = |Ao| + |sigma(a)|, hence |sigma(a)| = |Ao| mod 2 (mod 2 reduction of 2|a| = |Ao| + |sigma(a)|). Consequence: Sigma is contained in the affine hyperplane {sigma in {0,1}^D : |sigma| = |Ao| mod 2}, so |Sigma| <= 2^(|D|-1) for D nonempty, and rank_F M <= 2^(|D|-1). Scope: any partition satisfying the no-isolated-vertices hypothesis. This is an UPPER bound and does NOT lower-bound |Sigma|; it is recorded as a bookkeeping fact, not as progress toward G0006.

label: S0015
statement: SWITCHING LOWER BOUND (CLAIMED, session R1237). Setting: finite simple graph G=(V,E) with no isolated vertices; E = A disjoint-union B; D = V(A) cap V(B) (assumed nonempty); Ao = V(A)\V(B); Bo = V(B)\V(A). Valid row a: a matching inside A covering Ao. Valid column b: a matching inside B covering Bo. sigma(a) in {0,1}^D is the indicator of vertices of D covered by a. Sigma = {sigma(a): a valid and some valid b has sigma(b) = 1 - sigma(a)}. Claim: if G has a perfect matching M0 and r pairwise vertex-disjoint M0-alternating cycles C_1..C_r exist, each containing a vertex v_i in D whose two C_i-edges lie on different sides of the partition, then |Sigma| >= 2^r (hence rank_F M_{A,B} >= 2^r for every field F, by the rank identity S0001). PROOF. Step 1 (every PM splits): for a PM M, put a = M cap A and b = M cap B. Each v in Ao has all its G-edges in A, so a covers Ao, and b covers Bo likewise. For v in D exactly one M-edge meets v, and it lies in A or in B, so sigma(b) = 1 - sigma(a) on D. Hence sigma(M cap A) in Sigma for every PM M. Step 2 (flips): for S subset of [r], M_S = M0 symmetric-difference (union of E(C_i), i in S) is a PM: each vertex of C_i has one M0-edge and one non-M0 cycle edge, and flipping swaps them; vertices off the cycles are untouched. Step 3 (independent bits): v_i lies only on C_i, so the M_S-edge at v_i is the M0-edge e_i^0 if i not in S, and the non-M0 cycle edge e_i^1 if i in S. These two edges lie on different sides, so sigma(M_S cap A)_{v_i} = c_i XOR [i in S], where c_i = [e_i^0 in A]. Hence S -> sigma(M_S cap A) is injective (S and S' differ at v_i for any i in the symmetric difference), and by Step 1 its image lies in Sigma. So |Sigma| >= 2^r. QED. Consistency: each crossing vertex is in D, and |D| >= 2r, compatible with the parity bound |Sigma| <= 2^(|D|-1) (S0011, SURVIVED_REVIEW). Scope: uses only PERFECT MATCHINGS (a function in P), so the perfect-matching control applies and the lemma transfers to no non-P function.

label: S0024
statement: CLAIMED (R1287, claude-haiku-5-5). Restatement of S0015 for arbitrary r. Setting: G bipartite with parts A and B; M0 a perfect matching; C_1..C_r pairwise vertex-disjoint M0-alternating cycles; for each i a D-vertex v_i on C_i whose two C_i-edges go to different sides (one in A, one in B). For S subset of [r] let M_S = M0 xor (union of E(C_i) for i in S). Claims: (i) M_S is a perfect matching; (ii) the side of v_i under M_S is the side under M0 flipped iff i in S; (iii) the 2^r matchings M_S have pairwise distinct signatures, so |Sigma| >= 2^r. Proof of (i): a vertex outside the union of the C_i keeps its M0 edge. A vertex u on C_i has exactly one M0 edge and one non-M0 edge inside C_i (alternation), and the flip exchanges them, so u stays matched exactly once; vertex-disjointness means no vertex is affected by two cycles. Proof of (ii): v_i's M0 partner lies across one of its two cycle edges; after the flip its partner lies across the other, which is on the opposite side; cycles C_j, j != i, do not touch v_i. Proof of (iii): by (ii), the bits at v_1..v_r of the signature determine S, so the map S -> signature is injective. Membership of each signature in Sigma follows from (i): the A-part of M_S covers A-side vertices and the B-part covers the B side, as in the finite check cm-f4bb37887d0c4b7d. Assumption carried over from S0015: the signature records the side of each D-vertex. Not re-verified in this turn: the exact definition of Sigma as written in Q-3376c4c863.

statement: Proof: let z=(x,y), z'=(x',y') be nonzero with disjoint supports. (1) A nonzero vertex block x_v has support of size >=2, since its coordinates sum to 0 over GF(3). Two nonzero blocks x_v, x'_v cannot both occur, because two disjoint subsets of a 3-set of size >=2 do not exist. So the vertex sets A={v: x_v != 0} and A'={v: x'_v != 0} are disjoint. (2) Both are nonempty, since x=0 forces y=0. Pick a in A and b in A'; then x_b=0 and x'_a=0. (3) y_{ab,c}=-x_{a,c} in z, so it is nonzero iff c in supp(x_a); y'_{ab,c}=-x'_{b,c} in z', so it is nonzero iff c in supp(x'_b). Both sets have size >=2 inside {0,1,2}, so they meet at some c, giving a shared support coordinate. Contradiction. Dimension: vertex rows are independent and each edge row has a private y variable, so dim = 3n - n = 2n.

label: S0005
statement: Lemma R (range, c >= 1 fixed, beta > 0 fixed). There is n0(beta, c) such that for all n >= n0: 2^(beta n) / (c n) >= n. Proof. The inequality is equivalent to 2^(beta n) >= c n^2, i.e. beta n >= log2 c + 2 log2 n. (i) For n >= 16, log2 n <= sqrt(n): the function h(n) = sqrt(n) - log2 n has h(16) = 0 and h'(n) = 1/(2 sqrt n) - 1/(n ln 2) >= 0 for n >= 9 (since sqrt n >= 2/ln 2 there), so h >= 0 on [16, inf). (ii) Hence it suffices that beta n >= log2 c + 2 sqrt(n) for n >= 16. The left side is linear in n and the right side is o(n), so the set of failing n is finite; let n0(beta, c) be one more than its largest element (and at least 16). Then Lemma R holds for all n >= n0. QED. Scope: fixed beta > 0 and fixed c >= 1; the statement is asymptotic. It does not say the inequality holds for all n, and the failing set is non-empty (e.g. n = 15 for beta = 0.5, c = 1). Status: bookkeeping lemma for the MMW19 range reading, not progress toward P vs NP. Self-made and trivial: it does not count as progress under the owner rule.

structure.lemma: Finite-exception absorption (repair of the 'all n' range hypothesis in MMW19). Fix beta > 0, c >= 1, and let n0 = n0(beta,c) be the threshold from Lemma R, so that for all n >= n0, 2^(beta n)/(c n) >= n. Claim: if a one-pass streaming algorithm A decides Gap-MCSP[2^(beta n)/(c n), 2^(beta n)] (or its search version) for all n >= n0 using space S(N) and update time U(N), then there is a one-pass algorithm A' for all n >= 1 with space S(N) + K and update time U(N) + K, where K = K(beta,c) is a constant independent of n. Proof: for each of the finitely many lengths n < n0, the instance set is finite (truth tables of length 2^n < 2^n0). Hardcode the correct answers for those finitely many lengths into a fixed finite table, which costs a constant number of states. A' reads the input stream, identifies n from the input length, uses the table for n < n0 and runs A otherwise. Space and update time change by at most the constant K. QED. statement: LEMMA R2 (range absorption, beta > 0 and c >= 1 fixed). There is n0(beta,c) such that 2^(beta n)/(c n) >= n for all n >= n0. PROOF. The inequality is equivalent to g(n) := beta n - log2 c - 2 log2 n >= 0. For real x > 0, g'(x) = beta - 2/(x ln 2), which is positive for x > x0 := 2/(beta ln 2). Since beta > 0, g(x) -> infinity as x -> infinity, so there is n0 >= x0 with g(n0) >= 0. g is increasing on [n0, infinity), hence g(n) >= g(n0) >= 0 for all n >= n0. QED. A one-pass automaton that reads the stream, fixes n from the input length (length assumed known, as in MMW19), and hard-codes the answers for lengths below n0 needs K(beta,c) extra states, a constant. So A' has space S(N) + O(1) and update time U(N) + O(1). label: S0020
statement: Lemma R' (analytic range threshold, all n; closes sub-item G0009(b) only). Let beta > 0, c >= 1 and n0(beta,c) := max(16, 16/beta^2, 2*log2(c)/beta). Then for every integer n >= n0: 2^(beta n)/(c n) >= n. PROOF. The claim is equivalent to beta*n >= log2(c) + 2*log2(n). (i) For n >= 16, log2(n) <= sqrt(n): equality at n = 16 (4 = 4), and d/dn[sqrt(n) - log2(n)] = 1/(2 sqrt n) - 1/(n ln 2) >= 0 whenever sqrt(n) >= 2/ln 2, which holds for n >= 9. Hence it suffices to show beta*n >= log2(c) + 2 sqrt(n). (ii) Write beta*n = beta*n/2 + beta*n/2. For n >= 16/beta^2 we have sqrt(n) >= 4/beta, so beta*n/2 >= 2 sqrt(n). For n >= 2 log2(c)/beta we have beta*n/2 >= log2(c). Adding gives beta*n >= log2(c) + 2 sqrt(n) >= log2(c) + 2 log2(n). QED. Scope: all real beta > 0, c >= 1, all integers n >= n0. Not optimal: for beta = 1/10, c = 1 the bound gives n0 = 1600, while the grid last failure is n = 140 (multiples of the denominator only).

statement: LEMMA (explicit all-n absorption, for G0009(b)): for every real beta > 0, every real c >= 1, and every integer n >= N*(beta,c) := max(16, ceil(t0^2)) with t0 = (1 + sqrt(1 + beta*log2 c))/beta, we have 2^(beta n) >= c n^2, equivalently 2^(beta n)/(c n) >= n. statement:
statement_start: For every fixed cutoff B and language L on finite binary strings, if a one-pass machine A decides L on all inputs of length at least B using space S(N) and update time U(N), then there is a one-pass machine A' deciding L on all inputs, using S(N)+O_B(1) space and U(N)+O_B(1) update time.
lemma: Let B be fixed and L ⊆ {0,1}*. Suppose deterministic one-pass A decides L on every x with |x|≥B, using S(|x|) bits and update time U(|x|). Run A in parallel with a finite trie containing all binary strings of length <B and a dead state. Store 1_L(x) at each short-string leaf. At end, output the stored bit if the trie identifies a short string x; otherwise output A's answer. There are at most 2^B+1 trie states, so trie state and finite table use O_B(1) bits. Each update adds one constant-size trie transition, costing O_B(1) time. For |x|<B correctness follows from the table; for |x|≥B correctness follows from A's hypothesis. Thus A' decides L on all inputs using S(|x|)+O_B(1) bits and U(|x|)+O_B(1) update time. This repairs finite-exception bookkeeping only; it does not establish the OPS/MMW bridge.

lemma: Let B be fixed and L ⊆ {0,1}*. Suppose deterministic one-pass A decides L on every x with |x|≥B, using S(|x|) bits and update time U(|x|). Run A in parallel with a finite trie containing all binary strings of length <B and a dead state. Store 1_L(x) at each short-string leaf. At end, output the stored bit if the trie identifies a short string x; otherwise output A's answer. There are at most 2^B+1 trie states, so trie state and finite table use O_B(1) bits. Each update adds one constant-size trie transition, costing O_B(1) time. For |x|<B correctness follows from the table; for |x|≥B correctness follows from A's hypothesis. Thus A' decides L on all inputs using S(|x|)+O_B(1) bits and U(|x|)+O_B(1) update time. This repairs finite-exception bookkeeping only; it does not establish the OPS/MMW bridge.

statement_start: For every fixed beta>0 and c>0,
statement: For every fixed beta>0 and c>0, there exists N0 such that for every integer N>=N0, (log_2 N)^c <= N^beta. Proof: put x=log_2 N. It suffices to show x^c <= 2^(beta x). Taking base-2 logarithms, this is c log_2 x <= beta x. Since log_2 x / x tends to 0 as x tends to infinity, there is x0 such that c log_2 x <= beta x for all x>=x0. Taking N0=ceil(2^x0) proves the claim. Consequently the YES set MCSP[(log_2 N)^c] is contained in MCSP[N^beta] for N>=N0, under the same circuit-size measure and encoding. This is only threshold dominance; it gives no reduction and transfers no circuit lower bound between these languages.

statement: Lemma (finite-input repair). Fix a finite set of binary input strings F and a one-pass streaming decision procedure A for inputs outside F, with space S(N) and update time U(N). There is a one-pass procedure A' that decides any prescribed Boolean labeling of F and agrees with A outside F, using S(N)+O(1) space and U(N)+O(1) update time. Proof: Run A on every input while maintaining a finite-state tracker for membership in F. Such a tracker exists: use a trie of F, with a sink state once the observed prefix cannot be a prefix of any member of F. At end of input, if the tracker identifies a member x of F, output its prescribed label; otherwise output A's answer. The product state stores A's state and one of finitely many tracker states, adding only a constant number of bits and a constant-time tracker update. The constants may depend on F. For Gap-MCSP at a fixed cutoff n0, take F to be all input strings of lengths 2^n for n<n0 and label each promised instance by its exact Gap-MCSP answer (labels on non-promise inputs may be arbitrary). This repairs S0030's erroneous “one fixed bit per length” assertion: the finite table stores a label per input string. It only handles finitely many exceptional lengths and does not verify the magnification theorem's source hypotheses or close row A.

statement:
statement: Finite-exception repair for one-pass streaming decisions. Fix a finite set E of input strings and a Boolean labeling h:E->{0,1}. Suppose A is a one-pass streaming decider for a language L on every input outside E, using S(N) bits of space and U(N) update time at length N. There exists a one-pass machine A_h that decides L on all inputs, using S(N)+O_E(1) space and U(N)+O_E(1) update time. Proof: Build a finite-state prefix tracker T whose states are the prefixes of strings in E, plus a sink. On each symbol, T advances to the matching longer prefix if one exists, and enters the sink otherwise. At end of input, T identifies x when the full input x belongs to E; proper prefixes and the sink identify inputs outside E. Run A and T in parallel. Output h(x) for x in E and A’s output otherwise. A is correct outside E, and h gives the correct labels on E. The product adds only a fixed number of states, hence O_E(1) bits; each symbol update adds one fixed finite-state transition, hence O_E(1) time. For Gap-MCSP with fixed n0, E contains all truth-table encodings at lengths 2^n for n<n0; label each by its exact promised answer, extending arbitrarily to non-promise inputs. This repairs S0030: a finite table must distinguish each exceptional input, rather than store one bit per length. This is bookkeeping only; it verifies no source theorem and closes no bridge-map row.
scope: Finite exceptional input set E; A is correct outside E; constants may depend on E and h.

label: S0135
statement: statement: Finite-exception absorption, repaired. Fix integers L≥1 and a promise decision problem with binary inputs. Suppose a deterministic one-pass algorithm A decides it on every input of length N≥L, using at most S(N) bits of state and at most U(N) work per input bit. Then there is a deterministic one-pass algorithm A' deciding it on every finite binary input, using at most S(N)+O_L(1) bits of state and at most U(N)+O_L(1) work per input bit. Proof: for inputs of length less than L, build a binary trie containing every such string, with each terminal labeled by the problem's correct answer (or its promise status). This trie has fewer than 2^L nodes and therefore requires O(L) state bits. A' follows the trie while the input length is below L. In parallel it counts input length up to L; once length reaches L, it discards the trie state and simulates A on the stream, retaining A's state and the counter needed to select the branch. The counter uses O(log L) bits. At end of input, the trie branch returns its stored label and the simulation branch returns A's answer. Thus the added state and per-bit work are constants depending only on fixed L. This proves finite-exception absorption for a fixed cutoff; it does not establish any source theorem or row-A model match.

statement: Parameter translation for the published Gap-MCSP formula lower bound. Fix 0<alpha<2, and let d>1 be the constant from OPS Theorem 1.5. With N=2^n, the theorem's thresholds n^d and 2^{(alpha/2-o(1))n} are respectively (log_2 N)^d and N^{alpha/2-o(1)}, and its U_2-formula lower bound is N^{2-alpha}. Proof: n=log_2 N, so n^d=(log_2 N)^d and 2^{(alpha/2-o(1))n}=N^{alpha/2-o(1)} by exponentiation; the formula size is already stated as N^{2-alpha}. This is a parameter translation of Theorem 1.5 only, not a transfer to the general-circuit hypothesis of Theorem 1.4.

label: S0137
statement: Model-inclusion lemma (row A scope). For every Boolean function f and integer s>=1, if f has a U2-formula of size at most s, then f has a general Boolean circuit of size at most s, under the convention that a formula is a circuit with fan-out one and both models use the same gate basis. Proof: retain the formula's gates and wires as a circuit; every gate's output feeds its unique parent, so the computed function and gate count are unchanged. Thus a lower bound against U2-formulas does not rule out smaller general circuits with sharing, and OPS Theorem 1.5 alone does not establish Theorem 1.4's general-circuit premise.

label: S0138
statement: statement: Finite-prefix absorption for streaming decision. Let L≥1 be fixed, and let D be any promise decision problem on binary strings. If a deterministic one-pass streaming algorithm A decides D correctly on every promised input of length at least L, with state cost S(N) and per-bit work U(N), then there is a deterministic one-pass algorithm A′ deciding D on every promised input, with state cost S(N)+O_L(1) and per-bit work U(N)+O_L(1). Proof: There are finitely many binary strings of length less than L. Make a binary trie containing those strings, with each terminal labeled by D’s correct answer on promised inputs (and an arbitrary label on non-promised inputs). The trie has 2^L−1 nodes, a constant for fixed L. A′ tracks the trie state and a counter capped at L. If the stream ends before L, it returns the trie terminal’s label. If it reaches length L, it discards the trie state and simulates A on the stream, returning A’s answer at end. The capped counter and trie position use O_L(1) bits; trie transitions and the switch to A require O_L(1) additional work per bit. Hence the stated resource bounds hold. This repairs the refuted finite-exception step by storing a separate answer for each short input rather than assuming one answer per length.

label: S0141
statement: statement: Lemma (formula lower bound implies circuit-depth lower bound). Let f be computed by a fan-in-2 circuit of depth d, and suppose every fan-in-2 formula computing f has at least F gates. Unfold the circuit by making a fresh copy of a gate each time its output is used in the recursive expansion from the output gate. The result is a binary tree of depth at most d, with at most 2^{d+1}-1 nodes, and computes f. Hence F <= 2^{d+1}-1, so d >= log2(F+1)-1. In particular F=N^{2-alpha} implies d >= (2-alpha)log2(N)-1. Proof: each unfolded gate has at most two children, and the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of depth d is sum_{i=0}^d 2^i=2^{d+1}-1. The unfolding preserves the gate operation at every node and duplicates shared subcomputations, so its output is f. Apply the assumed formula lower bound and rearrange. This gives a depth consequence only; it does not imply a general-circuit size lower bound or P != NP.

statement:
statement: Lemma (explicit MMW threshold cutoff). Let 0< beta <=1 and c>=1 be fixed real constants, and set N=ceil(max{16/beta^2, 2 log_2(c)/beta}). For every integer n>=N, 2^(beta n)/(c n) >= n. Proof: Since n>=16/beta^2>=16, log_2(n)<=sqrt(n). Also n>=16/beta^2 implies sqrt(n)<=beta*n/4, hence 2 log_2(n)<=beta*n/2. The other cutoff gives log_2(c)<=beta*n/2. Therefore log_2(c)+2 log_2(n)<=beta*n; exponentiating base 2 gives c*n^2<=2^(beta*n), and division by c*n proves the claim. Consequently any failure of the range condition s(n)=2^(beta n)/(c n)>=n lies among the finitely many n<N. This lemma gives an explicit cutoff for the small-n range issue in the Q-34b02a6004 bridge audit; it makes no transfer claim.
proof: For n>=N, n>=16/beta^2>=16. For every n>=16, log_2 n<=sqrt(n), and sqrt(n)<=beta*n/4 follows by rearranging n>=16/beta^2. Thus 2log_2 n<=beta*n/2. Also n>=2log_2(c)/beta implies log_2(c)<=beta*n/2. Adding yields log_2(cn^2)<=beta*n, so cn^2<=2^(beta*n). As c,n are positive, divide by cn to obtain 2^(beta*n)/(cn)>=n.

statement: For fixed real constants beta>0 and c>0, there exists n0 such that for every integer n>=n0, 2^(beta*n)/(c*n)>=n; equivalently, the OPS threshold s(n)=2^(beta*n)/(c*n) satisfies the MMW size-range condition s(n)>=n eventually.
proof: Let a=2^beta>1. For n>=4, the binomial theorem gives a^n=(1+(a-1))^n >= binom(n,3)(a-1)^3 >= n^3(a-1)^3/24. Hence a^n>=c n^2 whenever n>=24c/(a-1)^3. Therefore n0=max(4,ceil(24c/(a-1)^3)) suffices. This proves only eventual numerical range inclusion, not theorem-quantifier compatibility or a lower-bound transfer.

statement: statement: Lemma (eventual threshold domination). For every fixed real beta>0 and c>0, there exists n0 such that for every integer n>=n0, 2^(beta*n)/(c*n) >= n. Proof: taking base-2 logarithms, this is equivalent to beta*n >= log2(c)+2log2(n). Since log2(n)/n and log2(c)/n tend to 0 for fixed c, choose n0 so that (log2(c)+2log2(n))/n <= beta for every n>=n0. Such an n0 exists by these limits. Thus the comparison threshold eventually meets s(n)>=n. The exact exponent remains beta*n-log2(c*n); this lemma does not identify the two threshold functions or bridge distinct theorem models.

statement: statement: Finite-exception absorption with parallel simulation. Fix an integer L≥1 and a promise decision problem on binary strings, with a specified correct output on every promised input. If a deterministic one-pass algorithm A is correct on every promised input of length N≥L, using at most S(N) state bits and U(N) work per input bit, then there is a deterministic one-pass algorithm A' correct on all promised inputs, using S(N)+O_L(1) state bits and U(N)+O_L(1) work per input bit. Proof: Build a finite binary trie for all strings of length less than L, labeling promised leaves by their correct outputs (and handling non-promised strings arbitrarily). Its size is a constant depending only on L. On each input, A' updates the trie state and simulates A from the first input bit, in parallel; it also counts the length up to L, using O(log L) bits. At end of input, if the length is less than L, it outputs the trie label; otherwise it outputs A's result. The simulation receives the entire input, including the first L bits. The trie, counter, and their per-bit updates add only O_L(1) state and work. Thus A' has the asserted resource bounds. This repairs the prior construction's gap, which switched to A only after consuming the first L bits.

statement: Lemma (eventual exponential threshold dominates every fixed polylog factor). For every real beta>0, c>=1 and fixed real k>=0, there exists N such that for every integer n>=N, 2^(beta*n)/(c*n) >= n*(log_2 n)^k. Proof: For n>=2, log_2(log_2 n)<=log_2 n. It suffices that beta*n >= log_2(c)+(2+k)*log_2(n). Since log_2(c)/n and log_2(n)/n tend to zero, choose N large enough that their weighted sum log_2(c)/n+(2+k)*log_2(n)/n <= beta for every n>=N; the terms are eventually decreasing. Then 2^(beta*n) >= c*n^2*(log_2 n)^k, and division by c*n proves the claim. This is only eventual threshold-range bookkeeping, not a CJSW/OPS transfer.

statement: Lemma (explicit finite-exception streaming simulation). Fix L>=1 and a promise language over binary strings, with a specified correct answer on each promised input of length <L. Suppose a deterministic one-pass machine A is correct on promised inputs of length at least L, with S state bits and update cost U per input bit. A' simulates A from the first input bit and also stores the input prefix while its length is <L, then switches to a saturated marker at length L. The 2^L-1 short prefixes plus one marker require L bits. At end, A' outputs a hardcoded correct answer for a short promised input; for inputs of length at least L it outputs A's answer. Thus A' uses S+L state bits and update cost U+O(L) per bit in a fan-in-2 bit model; for fixed L the finite output lookup has O_L(1) cost. Correctness follows by splitting on input length: below L, the stored prefix is the full input and the lookup gives its specified answer; at least L, A has processed the full input from the beginning and is correct by hypothesis. This repairs S0030's false per-length constant-answer assertion and does not establish any MCSP transfer.

statement: For any finite graph G=(V,L⊔R), let M have rows indexed by X⊆L and columns by Y⊆R, with M[X,Y]=1 iff X∪Y is a perfect matching. Let B be the vertices incident to at least one edge of L and at least one edge of R. Over every field, rank(M)≤2^{|B|}. Proof: A row indexed by X is zero unless X is a matching and covers every vertex incident only to L; likewise a column Y is zero unless Y is a matching and covers every vertex incident only to R. For nonzero rows and columns, X∪Y is a perfect matching exactly when the subsets of B covered by X and Y are disjoint and have union B. Thus compatibility depends only on the subset of B covered by X. Any two nonzero rows whose X cover the same subset of B agree on every column; zero rows also contribute no rank. There are at most 2^{|B|} distinct nonzero rows, so the row rank, hence the rank, is at most 2^{|B|}. This does not establish a lower bound for perfect matching or close a Route F obligation.

statement_start: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the satisfying assignments of Phi_G = AND_{uv in E} EXACT1(x_u,x_v,z_uv) project onto exactly the independent sets of G, and each projected assignment has a unique extension to the z variables.
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the satisfying assignments of Phi_G = AND_{uv in E} EXACT1(x_u,x_v,z_uv) project onto exactly the independent sets of G, and each projected assignment has a unique extension to the z variables. Proof: Fix an assignment x to V. For an edge uv, the equation x_u+x_v+z_uv=1 with all variables Boolean has a solution z_uv iff x_u+x_v<=1, equivalently not both endpoints are selected. When it has a solution, it is uniquely z_uv=1-x_u-x_v. Thus a satisfying extension exists iff x is an independent set, and then all auxiliary values are uniquely determined edge by edge. This also covers E empty, where every x is independent and there is exactly one empty assignment to z. Hence the projection is precisely the independent-set family and is bijective on extensions. This repairs the encoding boundary only; it does not establish any d-SDNNF lower bound or circuit lower bound.

label: S0005
statement: statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), let Psi_G = AND_{v in V} EXACT1(y_e : e incident to v), with one Boolean variable y_e per edge. The satisfying assignments of Psi_G are exactly the incidence vectors of perfect matchings of G. Proof: An assignment satisfying Psi_G selects exactly one incident edge at each vertex. Hence every vertex is covered, and no two selected edges share a vertex, so the selected edges form a perfect matching. Conversely, the incidence vector of any perfect matching selects exactly one incident edge at each vertex and satisfies every constraint. If G has an isolated vertex, both sets are empty. If G is empty, both consist of the unique empty assignment/matching. For cubic G, Psi_G has |E| variables, |V| constraints, and each variable occurs in exactly two constraints.

statement: statement: Lemma (cubic matching CNF encoding). Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple 3-regular graph, with one Boolean variable y_e for each edge. For each vertex v with incident edges e_1,e_2,e_3, encode EXACT1(y_e1,y_e2,y_e3) by the four clauses (y_e1 OR y_e2 OR y_e3), (NOT y_e1 OR NOT y_e2), (NOT y_e1 OR NOT y_e3), and (NOT y_e2 OR NOT y_e3). The resulting CNF has |E| variables, 4|V| clauses, clause width 2 or 3, and exactly six literal occurrences of each variable. Its satisfying assignments are exactly the incidence vectors of perfect matchings of G. Proof: The positive clause requires at least one incident edge variable to be true, and the three negative pair clauses prohibit two from being true. Together they require exactly one selected edge at v. Applying this at every vertex says precisely that the selected edges cover each vertex once, which is the definition of a perfect matching. Conversely, a perfect matching selects exactly one incident edge at every vertex, so satisfies all four clauses there. Each edge variable occurs in the four-clause block at each of its two endpoints; in each block it appears once positively and twice negatively, hence six literal occurrences total. Each block contributes four clauses, giving 4|V| clauses. This establishes the CNF encoding and its size/occurrence parameters only; it does not establish a d-SDNNF lower bound or any circuit lower bound.

statement: statement_start: For every finite simple graph G that is a disjoint union of even cycles and has n vertices, the Boolean perfect-matching function on edge variables has a deterministic decomposable NNF of size O(n). Proof: Write the components as cycles C_i of lengths 2k_i. Each C_i has exactly two perfect matchings, the two alternating edge sets A_i and B_i. For each matching M among these, form the term T_M that contains y_e for e in M and ¬y_e for every other edge of C_i. Set F_i=T_A_i∨T_B_i. Each term fixes all edge variables of C_i, so it accepts exactly one assignment; the two terms are disjoint, hence the disjunction is deterministic. Each term is a conjunction of distinct edge literals, so decomposable. A cycle has 2k_i literals per term, hence F_i has O(k_i) NNF nodes. Set F=∧_i F_i. Distinct components have disjoint edge-variable sets, so this conjunction is decomposable. An assignment satisfies F iff on each component it is one of that cycle's two alternating matchings, which is equivalent to being a perfect matching of G. Summing the O(k_i) sizes gives O(Σ_i k_i)=O(n).

structure.lemma: Lemma T (cut lemma, arbitrary gate semantics). Let C be a circuit over inputs x=(a,b), a in {0,1}^{n_A}, b in {0,1}^{n_B}, whose gates compute arbitrary Boolean functions of any fan-in. Let S be a set of gates closed under gate-predecessors (each gate input of a gate in S is in S or is an A-variable). Let kappa_E(S) be the number of wires into gates outside S that originate from an A-variable or from a gate in S. Then the number D of distinct rows of M_f[a,b]=f(a,b) satisfies log2 D <= kappa_E(S). Proof: each gate in S depends only on a, so the crossing-wire message m(a) in {0,1}^{kappa_E} is a function of a. Each gate outside S is a function of its in-neighbours (b-variables, A-variables, crossing wires, or outside gates), so by induction over outside gates f(a,b)=G(m(a),b). Row a is determined by m(a), hence D <= 2^{kappa_E}. If the output lies in S, f depends on a only and D=1.

statement: Cut rank bound with arbitrary gate semantics: for a circuit whose gates each compute an arbitrary function of their input wires (any fan-in), with T = number of wires owned by one side that feed a gate on the other side, rank_Q(M_f) <= 2^T for M_f[a,b]=f(a,b). statement: For n-bit Boolean f, if the residues of #SAT(f) modulo pairwise-coprime primes p_1,...,p_k are known and P=∏p_i>2^n, then these residues determine #SAT(f) uniquely and permit its exact reconstruction in time polynomial in n+Σ_i log p_i.
proof: Let z=#SAT(f), so 0≤z≤2^n. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a unique residue r in [0,P) matching all supplied residues. Since z<P, z is the unique integer in [0,P) with those residues, hence r=z. Standard CRT reconstruction uses polynomially many bit operations in the total input bit length. This proves only the reconstruction bridge; it does not establish the required tensor translation, contraction ranks, or their running time.

statement:
statement: Let F be a proper subset of {0,1}^N. Consider a deterministic, position-dependent streaming transducer that reads an N-bit string, has unrestricted transitions and decoder, and must output an object identifying the input truth table for every input in F and reject every input outside F. If distinct members of F require distinct output objects, then the minimum number of state bits is ceil(log2(|F|+1)).
evidence: Proof: At the final position, each f in F must lead to a state whose decoder outputs an object identifying f. Two distinct f,g cannot share a state, since a deterministic decoder on that state would have to identify both. Because F is proper, some y is outside F; its final state must decode as rejection, so it differs from every accepted final state. Thus at least |F|+1 states are necessary. Conversely, let S=ceil(log2(|F|+1)). At each position t, assign distinct codes to the extendable prefixes of members of F; there are at most |F| such prefixes, since each member contributes one prefix at t. Assign a further code to all non-extendable prefixes. For each position t and input bit b, define the transition on codes of reachable prefixes to the code of the resulting prefix (which is either extendable or non-extendable); define transitions arbitrarily on unreachable codes. At the end, decode each accepted member’s code as its identifying object and the non-extendable code as rejection. This uses at most |F|+1 states and establishes the matching upper bound.

statement:
statement: For every nonempty F subset of {0,1}^N with distinct required outputs for its members, there is a stationary deterministic streaming transducer that accepts exactly F, outputs the required identifying object on each f in F, rejects every input outside F, and uses |Pref(F)|+1 states, where Pref(F) is the set of all prefixes of members of F, including the full members.
evidence: Construct one state q_p for each p in Pref(F), plus a sink ⊥. Start at q_ε. On bit b from q_p, move to q_{pb} if pb is in Pref(F), otherwise move to ⊥; both transitions from ⊥ loop to ⊥. This is one position-independent transition function. After N bits, an input is in F exactly when its reached state is q_f for some f in F: every such path follows prefixes and reaches q_f, while any input not in F either leaves Pref(F) at some point and reaches ⊥, or would itself be a length-N member of F. Decode q_f as f's prescribed object and all other states as rejection. The construction has exactly |Pref(F)|+1 states.

statement:
statement: Let F be any subset of {0,1}^N, and let a deterministic transducer accept exactly F after reading N bits. For each t, define R_t(p)={u in {0,1}^{N-t}: pu is in F} for each length-t prefix p. Any such transducer, stationary or position-dependent, has at least |{R_t(p): p in {0,1}^t}| distinct states at layer t.
evidence: Proof: Fix t and prefixes p,q of length t with R_t(p) != R_t(q). By inequality of these sets, there is a suffix u of length N-t belonging to exactly one of R_t(p), R_t(q). If the transducer reached the same state after p and q, determinism implies that processing the identical suffix u from that state produces the same final state and hence the same acceptance decision. statement: Prop 5 (manuscript eq. (13)), all n: if F_E is unsatisfiable, A_E z = 1 is solvable over F_3, and deleting any single clause makes F_E satisfiable, then the rows of A_E (restricted to the n' occurring variables) are linearly independent over F_3, so rank = |E| and |E| <= n'-1.

label: S0002
statement: LEMMA Thm1-two-valued (manuscript eq. (3), all n>=3, E subset of T_n): F_E is satisfiable iff some z in A_E = {z in F_3^n : A_E z = 1} takes at most two values. Proof. (a) If x in {0,1}^n satisfies F_E, then each clause sum is an integer in {0..3} that is 1 mod 3, hence 1; so z = x in A_E has values in {0,1}. (b) Let z in A_E take at most two values, E nonempty (E empty: z=0). A constant value a gives clause sums 3a = 0 mod 3, not 1, so the value set is {0,1}, {0,2} or {1,2}. Case {0,1}: x = z is Boolean with clause sums 1. Case {0,2}: z = 2y, y Boolean; 2(y_a+y_b+y_c) = 1 mod 3 gives y_a+y_b+y_c = 2 exactly (range {0..3}); x = 1-y is Boolean with x_a+x_b+x_c = 1. label: S0004
statement:
statement: Lemma F_q (extension of manuscript Prop 14, eq. (40d)). Let q = p^k be a prime power and r, N >= 1 integers with r(q-1) < N. For every W in F_q^{r x N} there is z in {0,1}^N, z != 0, with Wz = 0 (the 0/1 vector is read in F_q^N).
derivation: (1) For j = 1..r put f_j(X) = sum_i W_{ji} X_i^{q-1} in F_q[X_1..X_N]. Each f_j is homogeneous of degree q-1, so sum_j deg f_j = r(q-1) < N. (2) Chevalley-Warning (valid over any finite field F_q of characteristic p): if sum_j deg f_j < N, the number of common zeros x in F_q^N of f_1..f_r is divisible by p. (3) The zero vector is a common zero, so the count is a positive multiple of p, hence at least p >= 2. Pick a common zero x != 0. (4) Set z_i = x_i^{q-1}. For x_i != 0 this is 1 (Lagrange in F_q^*), for x_i = 0 it is 0, so z in {0,1}^N, and z != 0 because x != 0. (5) (Wz)_j = sum_i W_{ji} x_i^{q-1} = f_j(x) = 0 for all j, so Wz = 0. QED. Remark: the prime case q = p is Prop 14; only the degree bound and the characteristic are used. Scope: linear W over F_q with r(q-1) < N; nothing on nonlinear, input-dependent or oracle-assisted updates, and nothing on manuscript eq. (8) or (40a).

statement: LEMMA (p=3, linear state, repair of manuscript Prop 14 / eq. 40d). Let W in F_3^{r x N} with N >= 2r+1. Then there is z in {0,1}^N, z != 0, with Wz = 0 and |supp z| <= 2r+1. Proof: let k = 2r+1 and W' the first k columns of W. Put P_j(X) = sum_{i<=k} W'_{ji} X_i^2 (j=1..r). Total degree 2r < k, so by Chevalley-Warning the number of common zeros in F_3^k is divisible by 3. The zero vector is one, so a nonzero common zero x exists. Set z_i = x_i^2 in {0,1} for i<=k and z_i = 0 otherwise. Then z != 0, Wz = 0, |supp z| <= k. QED. Corollary (promise restored, C=2): a t-sparse table on m variables has circuit size <= 2tm. If N = 2^m >= 2r+1 and C(2r+1)m <= s, the kernel vector z has circuit size <= s and shares its final state with the zero table, so an exact decoder with promise size s gives r >= min{2^{m-1}, ceil((s/(2m) - 1)/2)}. Scope: p=3, linear updates over F_3, exact decoders. Does not cover nonlinear or oracle-assisted updates, update time, eq. (8) or (40a). The exponential bound 2^{m-1} is NOT recovered; that needs a kernel vector of circuit size <= s with support near 2^m.

statement: LEMMA (REPAIR of S0001 / Prop 5, manuscript eq. (13); kind LEMMA; closes: none). Let n >= 3, E a subset of T_n, and r_i in F_3^n the 0/1 incidence row of clause i in E (three ones). Assume (H1) F_E is unsatisfiable; (H2) for every j in E, F_{E minus {j}} is satisfiable; (H3) A_E z = 1 has a solution z_0 in F_3^n. Let n' be the number of variables occurring in E. Then the rows r_i (i in E) are linearly independent over F_3, so |E| = rank A_E <= n' - 1. PROOF. (a) Suppose sum_{i in E} lambda_i r_i = 0 with some lambda_j != 0. For i != j the integer r_i . x lies in {0,1,2,3} and is 1 mod 3, hence equals 1. Dot the dependence with x: 0 = sum_{i != j} lambda_i + lambda_j (r_j . x) = lambda_j (r_j . x - 1), so r_j . x = 1 in F_3. The integer r_j . x in {0,1,2,3} is 1 mod 3, hence exactly 1, so x satisfies clause j. Thus x satisfies F_E, contradicting (H1). So the rows are independent and rank A_E = |E|. (d) Columns outside the n' occurring variables are zero, so rank is computed on those n' columns. Each row sums to 3 = 0 mod 3, so the all-ones vector on those columns is a nonzero kernel vector; rank <= n' - 1. Hence |E| <= n' - 1. QED. SCOPE: positive exact-one clauses over F_3 under (H1)-(H3). E empty violates (H1), so vacuous there. (H3) is used only in step (b) and is not derived here. NOT CLAIMED: any bound beyond |E| <= n'-1; nothing on manuscript eq. (8) or (40a). label: S0013
statement:
Prop 5′ (conditional rank lemma). Let E be a minimal unsatisfiable family of positive exact-one clauses, each involving three distinct variables, and let A_E be its incidence matrix over F_3 restricted to the n′ occurring variables. If A_E z = 1 has a solution z over F_3, then rank(A_E)=|E| and |E|≤n′−1.

Proof. Suppose the rows are dependent, so Σ_i λ_i r_i=0 for coefficients λ_i∈F_3 not all zero. Choose j with λ_j≠0. Taking the dot product with z gives Σ_i λ_i=0, since r_i·z=1 for every clause. Thus Σ_{i≠j}λ_i=−λ_j. For any w satisfying r_i·w=1 for all i≠j, the dependence gives λ_j(r_j·w)=−Σ_{i≠j}λ_i(r_i·w)=−Σ_{i≠j}λ_i=λ_j, hence r_j·w=1.

By minimality, there is a Boolean assignment x satisfying every clause except j. Apply the preceding implication to x. The integer sum of the three Boolean coordinates in clause j lies in {0,1,2,3}, and is congruent to 1 modulo 3. The only such value is 1. So x satisfies clause j as well, contradicting that E is unsatisfiable. The rows are therefore independent and rank(A_E)=|E|. Each row has three 1s, whose sum is 0 in F_3, so the all-ones vector lies in ker(A_E). It is nonzero because n′≥3. Rank-nullity now gives |E|=rank(A_E)≤n′−1. QED.

label: S0016
statement:
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the Boolean solutions (all variables in {0,1}) of the exact-one system (14)-(15) are in bijection with proper 3-colorings of G. Consequently the number of Boolean solutions equals the number of proper 3-colorings.
derivation: Given a Boolean solution, each vertex equation (14) has exactly one selected color c, defining a coloring. For each edge e={u,v} and color c, equation (15) forces y_{e,c}=1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c}. This forced value is in {0,1} exactly when x_{u,c}+x_{v,c}<=1, which for one-hot vertex indicators is equivalent to u and v not both having color c. Requiring this for all c is equivalent to the endpoints having different colors, so the coloring is proper. Conversely, from any proper 3-coloring set x_{v,c}=1 exactly at its color and set y_{e,c}=1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c}; properness ensures every y is Boolean and all equations hold. Both constructions are inverse because all x are fixed by the coloring and all y are forced by (15), proving a bijection.

structure.evidence: The derivation above proves both directions and uniqueness of the slack variables; finite corroboration experiment to be cited after execution.

statement:
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the homogeneous kernel over F_3 of the coefficient matrix of (14)-(15) has exactly 3^(2|V|) vectors. Proof: For each vertex v choose a triple (a_v,0,a_v,1,a_v,2) with coordinate sum 0 in F_3; there are 3^2 independent choices per vertex. Define every edge coordinate by b_{uv,c}=-a_{u,c}-a_{v,c}. Then each vertex homogeneous equation holds by the triple-sum condition, and each edge homogeneous equation holds by definition. Conversely, every kernel vector must have vertex triples summing to 0 and every edge coordinate forced by that same formula. Thus these choices give a bijection between (F_3^2)^V and the kernel, proving the count.
derivation: The construction and inverse are explicit and use only the coefficient equations in (14)-(15), not claimed steps S0013 or S0016.

statement:
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the fraction of solutions to the affine system (14)-(15) over F_3 whose coordinates all lie in {0,1} is chi_G(3)/3^(2|V|), where chi_G(3) denotes the number of proper 3-colorings of G.
derivation: For each vertex, the affine equation requires its three coordinates to sum to 1 in F_3. There are nine such triples, of which exactly three are Boolean: the one-hot triples. Choosing a Boolean triple at each vertex selects a color. For each edge and color, equation (15) uniquely forces y=1-x_u-x_v in F_3. This value is Boolean for all colors exactly when the endpoints have different selected colors: if both select the same color then the corresponding slack is -1=2, not Boolean; otherwise all slacks are 0 or 1. Hence Boolean affine solutions are in bijection with proper 3-colorings. The affine system has 3^(2|V|) solutions by the recorded affine-count argument (S0018); equivalently, each vertex triple has nine choices and every edge coordinate is forced. Dividing the Boolean-solution count chi_G(3) by the total gives the claimed fraction.

statement:
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E) and every finite field F_q of characteristic greater than 3, the affine system (14)-(15) over F_q has q^(2|V|) solutions, exactly chi_G(3) of which have every coordinate in {0,1}.
derivation: For each vertex, choose x_{v,0},x_{v,1} freely and let equation (14) force x_{v,2}; this gives q^2 choices per vertex. Every edge coordinate is uniquely forced by (15), so there are q^(2|V|) total solutions. Since char(F_q)>3, a triple of Boolean coordinates sums to 1 in F_q exactly when its integer sum is 1, so Boolean vertex triples are precisely the one-hot triples and select a color. The forced edge slack 1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c} is Boolean for all colors exactly when the endpoints select different colors. Thus Boolean solutions correspond bijectively to proper 3-colorings, giving exactly chi_G(3) Boolean solutions.

label: S0021
statement: Lemma (forest count for the manuscript encoding). Let G=(V,E) be a finite forest, with c connected components and n=|V|. For the Boolean exact-one system (14)-(15), the number of solutions is 3^c 2^(n-c). Proof: By the encoding bijection to proper 3-colorings, it suffices to count colorings componentwise. In each tree component choose a root: it has 3 choices. Orient every edge away from the root. Each non-root vertex has exactly one parent, and once the parent color is fixed, it has exactly 2 choices different from that color; because a tree has no other already-colored neighbor, these choices are independent. Thus a tree on t vertices has 3*2^(t-1) proper 3-colorings. Multiplying over components gives product_i 3*2^(t_i-1)=3^c 2^(n-c). Isolated vertices are included as one-vertex trees and contribute 3. This establishes the claimed exact solution count for every forest, including the empty forest (n=c=0, count 1).

statement:
statement: For every finite forest G=(V,E) with n vertices and c connected components, and every integer q>=1, the number of proper q-colorings of G is q^c(q-1)^(n-c), with the empty forest count interpreted as 1.
derivation: Proof: In each component choose a root and orient edges away from it. Each root has q choices. For each non-root vertex, after its parent is colored, exactly q-1 colors remain available. Since a forest has a unique root-to-vertex path and no additional edges between already assigned vertices that impose new constraints at this stage, these choices are independent in a root-first ordering. A component with t vertices therefore has q(q-1)^(t-1) colorings. Multiplying over components gives q^c(q-1)^(sum_i(t_i-1))=q^c(q-1)^(n-c). For the empty forest the unique empty coloring gives 1.

label: S0028
statement:
statement: Cactus coloring product lemma. Let G be a finite cactus graph (each edge belongs to at most one simple cycle), with connected components G_1,...,G_c. For any integer q>=2, the number of proper q-colorings is the product over components of q times the product over their blocks B of P_B(q)/q, where P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1) for a cycle block of length ell. The empty graph has one coloring.
evidence: Proof: In a connected cactus, the incidence graph of blocks and articulation vertices is a tree. Root it at any block and choose a coloring of the root, with P_root(q) choices. Each later block meets the exposed subgraph at one articulation vertex. Color symmetry implies exactly P_B(q)/q extensions for each fixed color at that vertex. The block tree ensures new blocks add disjoint vertices and impose no other constraints. Multiplying gives q times the product of P_B(q)/q over blocks. A bridge has q(q-1) colorings. A cycle of length ell has tr((J-I)^ell)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1), since J-I has eigenvalues q-1 once and -1 with multiplicity q-1. Components color independently; the empty graph has one coloring. The proof-state response showed no matching open obligation id, so this lemma does not claim to close a pre-recorded obligation.

label: S0029
statement:
statement: Polynomial cactus chromatic formula. Let G be a finite cactus graph with connected components G_1,...,G_c, and let B range over all its blocks; write ell(B) for the cycle length of a cycle block. As a polynomial identity in Z[q], its chromatic polynomial is chi_G(q)= product_{i=1}^c [ q * product_{B in blocks(G_i)} (P_B(q)/q) ], where P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell(B)+(-1)^ell(B)(q-1) for a cycle block. The empty graph has chromatic polynomial 1.
evidence: Proof: For every integer q>=2, the block-cut incidence graph of each connected cactus is a tree. Root it at a block. Starting with a coloring of the root block, expose blocks in tree order; each new block meets the already exposed graph at exactly its parent articulation vertex and has no other previously exposed vertices. For any fixed color at this vertex, the number of proper extensions to the new block is P_B(q)/q: color permutations act transitively on the q possible fixed colors, and summing the extension counts over all q colors gives P_B(q), the total number of colorings of B. The bridge and cycle formulas for P_B(q) follow respectively from q(q-1) and tr((J-I)^ell)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1). Thus the displayed identity holds for every integer q>=2. Each cycle quotient P_B(q)/q is an integer polynomial, as follows from P_B(q)/q=sum_{j=0}^{ell-1}(-1)^j(q-1)^(ell-1-j). Both sides are therefore polynomials and, since they agree at infinitely many integers, are identical. Components color independently; the empty graph has polynomial 1. This closes no pre-recorded PNP-001 obligation.

label: S0030
statement:
statement: Corrected polynomial cactus chromatic formula. Let G be a finite cactus graph, with connected components G_i and blocks B. For each cycle block B of length ell>=3 set C_B(q)=sum_{j=0}^{ell-2}(-1)^j(q-1)^(ell-1-j); for each bridge block set C_B(q)=q-1. Then in Z[q], chi_G(q)=product_i [q * product_{B in blocks(G_i)} C_B(q)]. The empty graph has chromatic polynomial 1.
evidence: Proof: For each integer q>=2, root the block-cut tree of a connected cactus at a block and expose blocks in tree order. Each added block meets the exposed graph only at its parent articulation vertex. Color permutations act transitively on the q choices for that vertex, so the number of extensions for any fixed color is the block's chromatic polynomial divided by q. A bridge contributes q(q-1), hence quotient q-1. A cycle of length ell contributes (q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1). Writing x=q-1, this is x(x^(ell-1)+(-1)^ell); division by q=x+1 gives sum_{j=0}^{ell-2}(-1)^j x^(ell-1-j), as is verified by multiplying the finite alternating sum by x+1. Thus the product formula holds for every integer q>=2. Each factor is in Z[q], and the two sides are polynomials agreeing at infinitely many integers, so they are identical. Components color independently; the empty graph has polynomial 1. Repair note: the expansion recorded in S0029 used upper index ell-1, adding an erroneous final constant term; the corrected upper index is ell-2.
